title: Fast charging explained: why your phone slows near the end
description: Fast charging can fill a dead phone battery in under 25 minutes, but how does it actually work? This short explains the simple physics behind charging speed, why your phone deliberately slows down near full — usually around 80% — and why your charger, cable and phone chip all have to match. You'll also see what modern phones do overnight to protect battery health. No jargon: one equation and one analogy that make it click.

scenes.say: Guess how many minutes a 100W charger needs to go from dead to full. Take a guess.
Under 25 minutes. And a standard charger from five years ago? Nearly three hours.
One equation: Watts equals Volts times Amps. Volts is how hard it pushes; Amps is how much charge flows each second. Together, that's Watts — energy flowing each second.
An old charger does 5 Watts. A fast one pushes 27 or 100. More watts, more energy each second.
Here's the trick — your battery changes behavior around 80%. Think of a bicycle tyre: first 30 pumps fly in, last 10 push back.

visual.note: First pumps easy — last ones push back

scenes.say: Inside the battery, near full, forcing charge in builds heat, and heat ages it — so the phone eases off. Usually near 80%, some phones wait till 85 or 90.

scenes.say: Fast charging needs three things: the charger, the cable, and a tiny chip in your phone that controls charging.
They compare speeds. Like a relay team, the slowest sets the pace — a cheap cable limits a 100W charger.
Will fast charging wreck my battery? Not with normal use. Many phones learn your routine — they hold 80% overnight, then finish before you wake.
Fast charging is fine — the slowest link sets the pace. Drop your guess. Thoma out!
